    28                  Proclamation 10947 of June 3, 2025
    29  
    30                  
    31  Adjusting Imports of Aluminum and Steel Into the 
    32                  United States
    33  
    34                  By the President of the United States of America
    35  
    36                  A Proclamation
    37  
    38                  1. On January 11, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    39                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on the 
    40                  Secretary's investigation into the effect of imports of 
    41                  steel mill articles (steel articles) on the national 
    42                  security of the United States under section 232 of the 
    43                  Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended (19 U.S.C. 
    44                  1862) (section 232). The Secretary found and advised me 
    45                  of his opinion that steel articles are being imported 
    46                  into the United States in such quantities and under 
    47                  such circumstances as to threaten to impair the 
    48                  national security of the United States.
    49  
    50                  2. In Proclamation 9705 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    51                  Imports of Steel Into the United States), and 
    52                  Proclamation 9980 of January 24, 2020 (Adjusting 
    53                  Imports of Derivative Aluminum Articles and Derivative 
    54                  Steel Articles Into the United States), I concurred 
    55                  with the Secretary's findings that steel articles, as 
    56                  defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9705, and 
    57                  derivative steel articles, as described in clause 3 of 
    58                  Proclamation 9980, are being imported into the United 
    59                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    60                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    61                  United States, and I decided to adjust the imports of 
    62                  those steel articles and derivative steel articles by 
    63                  imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    64                  articles imported from most countries. In Proclamation 
    65                  10896 of February 10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Steel 
    66                  Into the United States), I decided to adjust the 
    67                  imports of steel articles and derivative steel articles 
    68                  by imposing a 25 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    69                  articles imported from all countries.
    70  
    71                  3. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary transmitted to me 
    72                  a report on the Secretary's investigation into the 
    73                  effect of imports of aluminum articles on the national 
    74                  security of the United States under section 232. The 
    75                  Secretary found and advised me of his opinion that 
    76                  aluminum articles are being imported into the United 
    77                  States in such quantities and under such circumstances 
    78                  as to threaten to impair the national security of the 
    79                  United States.
    80  
    81                  4. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    82                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), and 
    83                  Proclamation 9980, I concurred with the Secretary's 
    84                  findings that aluminum articles, as defined in clause 1 
    85                  of Proclamation 9704, and derivative aluminum articles, 
    86                  as described in clause 3 of Proclamation 9980, are 
    87                  being imported into the United States in such 
    88                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    89                  to impair the national security of the United States, 
    90                  and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum articles 
    91                  and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 10 
    92                  percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    93                  from most countries. In Proclamation 10895 of February 
    94                  10, 2025 (Adjusting Imports of Aluminum Into the United 
    95                  States), I decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    96                  articles and derivative aluminum articles by imposing a 
    97                  25 percent ad valorem tariff on such articles imported 
    98                  from all countries.
    99  
   100                  5. In Proclamation 10896 and Proclamation 10895, I 
   101                  instructed the Secretary to continue to monitor imports 
   102                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   103                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   104                  respectively, and
   105  
   106  [[Page 24200]]
   107  
   108                  to review the status of such imports with respect to 
   109                  the national security of the United States. The 
   110                  Secretary has done so and has advised me accordingly.
   111  
   112                  6. After considering current information newly provided 
   113                  by the Secretary, among other things, I have determined 
   114                  that it is necessary to increase the previously 
   115                  described steel and aluminum tariffs to adjust the 
   116                  imports of steel and aluminum articles and their 
   117                  derivative articles so that such imports will not 
   118                  threaten to impair the national security. In my 
   119                  judgment, the increased tariffs will more effectively 
   120                  counter foreign countries that continue to offload low-
   121                  priced, excess steel and aluminum in the United States 
   122                  market and thereby undercut the competitiveness of the 
   123                  United States steel and aluminum industries. Although 
   124                  the previously imposed steel and aluminum tariffs have 
   125                  helped provide critical price support in the United 
   126                  States market, they have not yet enabled these 
   127                  industries to develop and maintain the rates of 
   128                  capacity production utilization that are necessary for 
   129                  the industries' sustained health and for projected 
   130                  national defense needs. I have determined that 
   131                  increasing the previously imposed tariffs will provide 
   132                  greater support to these industries and reduce or 
   133                  eliminate the national security threat posed by imports 
   134                  of steel and aluminum articles and their derivative 
   135                  articles.
   136  
   137                  7. Accordingly, I have determined that it is necessary 
   138                  and appropriate to increase the tariff rate for imports 
   139                  of steel articles and derivative steel articles, and 
   140                  aluminum articles and derivative aluminum articles, 
   141                  from 25 percent ad valorem to 50 percent ad valorem 
   142                  effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   143                  June 4, 2025. I have also determined that it is 
   144                  necessary and appropriate to modify the way in which 
   145                  the tariff measures described in Executive Order 14289 
   146                  of April 29, 2025 (Addressing Certain Tariffs on 
   147                  Imported Articles), apply to steel articles and 
   148                  derivative steel articles, and aluminum articles and 
   149                  derivative aluminum articles, to ensure the 
   150                  effectiveness of the tariff changes described in this 
   151                  proclamation and the alignment of policy priorities 
   152                  between this proclamation and Executive Order 14289. I 
   153                  have further determined that it is necessary and 
   154                  appropriate to allow for the implementation of the 
   155                  U.S.-UK Economic Prosperity Deal of May 8, 2025 (EPD), 
   156                  and to accordingly provide different treatment, as 
   157                  described below, for imports of steel and aluminum 
   158                  articles, and their derivatives, from the United 
   159                  Kingdom.
   160  
   161                  8. Section 232 authorizes the President to adjust the 
   162                  imports of an article and its derivatives that are 
   163                  being imported into the United States in such 
   164                  quantities or under such circumstances as to threaten 
   165                  to impair the national security.
   166  
   167                  9. Section 604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (19 
   168                  U.S.C. 2483), authorizes the President to embody in the 
   169                  Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) 
   170                  the substance of statutes affecting import treatment, 
   171                  and actions thereunder, including the removal, 
   172                  modification, continuance, or imposition of any rate of 
   173                  duty or other import restriction.
   174  
   175                  NOW, THEREFORE, I, DONALD J. TRUMP, President of the 
   176                  United States of America, by the authority vested in me 
   177                  by the Constitution and the laws of the United States 
   178                  of America, including section 232; the International 
   179                  Emergency Economic Powers Act (50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.); 
   180                  section 301 of title 3, United States Code; and section 
   181                  604 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended, do hereby 
   182                  proclaim as follows:
   183  
   184                      (1) As set forth in Annexes I and II to this 
   185                  proclamation, as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight time on 
   186                  June 4, 2025, the tariffs proclaimed by Proclamation 
   187                  9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as amended; 
   188                  Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 10895; and 
   189                  Proclamation 10896 are modified to increase the 
   190                  respective tariff rates from an additional 25 percent 
   191                  ad valorem to an additional 50 percent ad valorem.
   192                      (2) The modifications to the HTSUS made by clause 1 
   193                  of this proclamation shall be effective with respect to 
   194                  goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn from 
   195                  warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   196                  eastern
   197  
   198  [[Page 24201]]
   199  
   200                  daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall continue in 
   201                  effect, unless such actions are expressly reduced, 
   202                  modified, or terminated.
   203                      (3) Any imports of articles set forth in Annex II 
   204                  to this proclamation that were admitted into a United 
   205                  States foreign trade zone under ``privileged foreign 
   206                  status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.41 before 12:01 a.m. 
   207                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, shall be subject 
   208                  upon entry for consumption made on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   209                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, to the 
   210                  provisions of the tariff in effect at the time of the 
   211                  entry for consumption.
   212                      (4) Any article set forth in Annex I to this 
   213                  proclamation, except those eligible for admission under 
   214                  ``domestic status'' as defined in 19 CFR 146.43, that 
   215                  is subject to a duty imposed by this proclamation and 
   216                  that is admitted into a United States foreign trade 
   217                  zone on or after June 4, 2025, may be admitted only 
   218                  under ``privileged foreign status'' as defined in 19 
   219                  CFR 146.41, and will be subject upon entry for 
   220                  consumption to any ad valorem rates of duty related to 
   221                  the classification under the applicable HTSUS 
   222                  subheading.
   223                      (5) Effective as of 12:01 a.m. eastern daylight 
   224                  time on June 4, 2025, Executive Order 14289 is amended 
   225                  by revising section 3(a)(ii) to read as follows: ``(ii) 
   226                  An article subject to tariffs pursuant to the actions 
   227                  listed in section 2(d) or 2(e) of this order shall not 
   228                  be subject to additional tariffs on that article 
   229                  pursuant to the actions listed in section 2(b) or 2(c) 
   230                  of this order.'' As set forth in Annex III of this 
   231                  proclamation, this amendment shall be effective with 
   232                  respect to goods entered for consumption, or withdrawn 
   233                  from warehouse for consumption, on or after 12:01 a.m. 
   234                  eastern daylight time on June 4, 2025, and shall 
   235                  continue in effect, unless such actions are expressly 
   236                  reduced, modified, or terminated.
   237                      (6) Notwithstanding any prior proclamation or 
   238                  Executive Order, the non-aluminum, non-steel content of 
   239                  all aluminum and steel articles and derivative articles 
   240                  shall be subject to tariffs pursuant to Executive Order 
   241                  14257 of April 2, 2025 (Regulating Imports With a 
   242                  Reciprocal Tariff To Rectify Trade Practices That 
   243                  Contribute to Large and Persistent Annual United States 
   244                  Goods Trade Deficits), as amended, and any other 
   245                  applicable tariffs. The additional ad valorem duties 
   246                  described in clause 1 and clause 7 of this proclamation 
   247                  shall apply only to the steel content of articles in 
   248                  Chapter 73 of the HTSUS and only to the aluminum 
   249                  content of articles in Chapter 76 of the HTSUS. U.S. 
   250                  Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall issue 
   251                  authoritative guidance mandating strict compliance with 
   252                  declaration requirements for steel and aluminum content 
   253                  in imported articles and outlining maximum penalties 
   254                  for noncompliance, including that importers who submit 
   255                  underreported declarations may be subject to severe 
   256                  consequences, including but not limited to significant 
   257                  monetary penalties, loss of import privileges, and 
   258                  criminal liability, consistent with United States law.
   259                      (7) Notwithstanding clause 1 of this proclamation, 
   260                  the applicable rates of duty for articles of the United 
   261                  Kingdom that would otherwise be applicable pursuant to 
   262                  Proclamation 9704, as amended; Proclamation 9705, as 
   263                  amended; Proclamation 9980, as amended; Proclamation 
   264                  10895; and Proclamation 10896 shall remain at 25 
   265                  percent ad valorem. On or after July 9, 2025, the 
   266                  Secretary may adjust the applicable rates of duty and

tools.description: Metadata for one Federal Register document: title, type, action, citation, page range, publication/signing/effective dates, comment deadline, docket, RIN, CFR parts affected, corrections, abstract.

tools.name: fr_toc
tools.description: Outline of a document's full text: headings with line numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_grep

pattern.description: Python regular expression, searched over the whole text (a match may span lines). ^ and $ match at line boundaries; . does not match a newline.
pattern.title: Pattern

context.description: Lines of context around each match (default 2, at most 10).
context.title: Context

tools.description: Regex search inside one document's full text. Shows the lines of each match with line numbers, context lines and the FR page of each match. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

tools.name: fr_text
tools.description: Read a document's full text by line range, with line numbers. [[Page N]] markers give FR page numbers. Output may contain CLI-style hints such as '--start N' or '--max'; they refer to this tool's parameters.

answer.description: Direct answer to each lettered part, in order, labelled (a), (b), ...
answer.title: Answer

basis.description: Provisions and documents relied on, with citations.
basis.title: Basis

uncertainty.description: What the documents leave open, or "None".
uncertainty.title: Uncertainty

    65                  By the President of the United States of America
    66  
    67                  A Proclamation
    68  
    69                  1. On January 19, 2018, the Secretary of Commerce 
    70                  (Secretary) transmitted to me a report on his 
    71                  investigation into the effect of imports of aluminum 
    72                  articles on the national security of the United States 
    73                  under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, 
    74                  as amended (19 U.S.C. 1862). The Secretary found and 
    75                  advised me of his opinion that aluminum articles were 
    76                  being imported into the United States in such 
    77                  quantities and under such circumstances as to threaten 
    78                  to impair the national security of the United States.
    79  
    80                  2. In Proclamation 9704 of March 8, 2018 (Adjusting 
    81                  Imports of Aluminum Into the United States), I 
    82                  concurred in the Secretary's finding that aluminum 
    83                  articles were being imported into the United States in 
    84                  such quantities and under such circumstances as to 
    85                  threaten to impair the national security of the United 
    86                  States, and decided to adjust the imports of aluminum 
    87                  articles, as defined in clause 1 of Proclamation 9704, 
    88                  by imposing a 10 percent ad valorem tariff on such 
    89                  articles imported from most countries.
    90  
    91                  3. In Proclamation 9704, I further stated that any 
    92                  country with which we have a security relationship is 
    93                  welcome to discuss with the United States alternative 
    94                  ways to address the threatened impairment of the 
    95                  national security caused by imports from that country, 
    96                  and noted that, should the United States and any such 
    97                  country arrive at a satisfactory alternative means to 
    98                  address the threat to the national security such that I 
    99                  determine that imports from that country no longer 
   100                  threaten to impair the national security, I may remove 
   101                  or modify the restriction on aluminum articles imports 
   102                  from that country and, if necessary, adjust the tariff 
   103                  as it applies to other countries, as the national 
   104                  security interests of the United States require.
   105  
   106                  4. The United States has successfully concluded 
   107                  discussions with Canada and Mexico on satisfactory 
   108                  alternative means to address the threatened impairment 
   109                  of the national security posed by aluminum imports from 
   110                  Canada and Mexico. The United States has agreed on a 
   111                  range of measures with Canada and Mexico to prevent the 
   112                  importation of aluminum that is unfairly subsidized or 
   113                  sold at dumped prices, to prevent the transshipment of 
   114                  aluminum, and to monitor for and avoid import surges. 
   115                  These measures are expected to allow imports of 
   116                  aluminum from Canada and Mexico to remain stable at 
   117                  historical levels without meaningful increases, thus 
   118                  permitting the domestic capacity utilization to remain 
   119                  reasonably commensurate with the target level 
   120                  recommended in the Secretary's report. In my judgment, 
   121                  these measures will provide effective, long-term 
   122                  alternative means to address the contribution of these 
   123                  countries' imports to the threatened impairment of the 
   124                  national security.
   125  
   126                  5. In light of these agreements, I have determined 
   127                  that, under the framework in the agreements, imports of 
   128                  aluminum from Canada and Mexico will no longer threaten 
   129                  to impair the national security, and thus I have 
   130                  decided to exclude Canada and Mexico from the tariff 
   131                  proclaimed in Proclamation 9704, as amended. The United 
   132                  States will monitor the implementation and 
   133                  effectiveness of these measures in addressing our 
   134                  national security needs, and I may revisit this 
   135                  determination as appropriate.
   136  
   137  [[Page 23984]]
   138  
   139                  6. In light of my determination to exclude, on a long-
   140                  term basis, these countries from the tariff proclaimed 
   141                  in Proclamation 9704, as amended, I have considered 
   142                  whether it is necessary and appropriate in light of our 
   143                  national security interests to make any corresponding 
   144                  adjustments to such tariff as it applies to other 
   145                  countries. I have determined that, in light of the 
   146                  agreed-upon measures with Canada and Mexico, it is 
   147                  necessary and appropriate, at this time, to maintain

  "Q1": {
    "answer": "(a) The section 338 presidential series comprises the following ten proclamations. All dates in the table are in 2026; all stated times are Eastern.

| Proclamation; FR document; first-page citation | Signed; published | Operative action and application event |
|---|---|---|
| **11046**; **2026-14991**; **91 FR 46639** | July 20; July 23 | Imposes 50% additional duty on its Annex II Canadian products concerning alcoholic-beverage discrimination. Clauses (1) and (3) originally specify **August 19, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption; 11056 subsequently changes commencement to August 22. |
| **11047**; **2026-14992**; **91 FR 46653** | July 20; July 23 | Corresponding 50% duty concerning dairy discrimination, with the same original **August 19, 12:01 a.m.** consumption-entry/warehouse-withdrawal trigger, subsequently postponed to August 22. |
| **11048**; **2026-14997**; **91 FR 46663** | July 20; July 23 | Corresponding 50% duty concerning motor-vehicle discrimination, with the same original **August 19, 12:01 a.m.** consumption-entry/warehouse-withdrawal trigger, subsequently postponed to August 22. |
| **11056**; **2026-17294**; **91 FR 54789** | August 18; August 24 | Postpones all three duties to **August 22, 12:01 a.m.** The underlying consumption-entry/warehouse-withdrawal triggers remain applicable. It expressly replaces the effective date in each original Annex II chapeau. |
| **11061**; **2026-18835**; **91 FR 58311** | September 8; September 14 | Excludes its Annex Canadian alcoholic beverages from importation beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, not consumption entry. Previously imported but unentered goods remain subject to 50% duty. |
| **11062**; **2026-18836**; **91 FR 58319** | September 8; September 14 | Corresponding dairy-related Annex import exclusion beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, with the same prior-import grandfathering. |
| **11063**; **2026-18837**; **91 FR 58325** | September 8; September 14 | Corresponding motor-vehicle-related Annex import exclusion beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, with the same prior-import grandfathering. |
| **11064**; **2026-18838**; **91 FR 58331** | September 8; September 14 | Adds Annex I Part A products to the alcoholic-beverage-related duty, removes Part B products, and makes the duty cumulative with section 232 duties, beginning **September 15, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |
| **11065**; **2026-18839**; **91 FR 58339** | September 8; September 14 | Adds Annex I Part A products to the motor-vehicle-related duty, removes Part B products, and makes the duty cumulative with section 232 duties, beginning **September 15, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |
| **11076**; **2026-22292**; **91 FR 68861** | October 23; October 30 | Further changes motor-vehicle-related coverage: **Part A removes**, **Part B adds** products. Continues section 232 stacking. Applies beginning **October 30, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |

The original three proclamations also have separate foreign-trade-zone provisions governing admission on or after their effective date; those are not the consumption-entry trigger for collecting the duty.

(b) **Product-coverage changes:**

- **Alcoholic-beverage action:** 11046 establishes the original Annex II coverage and readable exceptions; 11064 adds Part A, removes Part B, and eliminates the section 232 non-stacking treatment; 11061 switches its Annex goods from additional-duty treatment to an import prohibition for new imports, while preserving 50% treatment for prior imports.
- **Dairy action:** 11047 establishes original coverage and exceptions; 11062 switches its Annex goods to an import prohibition for new imports. No actual dairy scope-modification proclamation was located. In particular, the original section 232 exception was not removed by a published dairy scope proclamation.
- **Motor-vehicle action:** 11048 establishes original coverage and exceptions; 11065 adds Part A, removes Part B, and permits section 232 stacking; 11063 switches its Annex goods to an import prohibition for new imports; 11076 subsequently removes its Part A and adds its Part B.
- **11056 changes timing, not product coverage.**",

Postponement: 11056, clause (1), FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790. Import exclusions: 11061, clauses (1)–(3), FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58312–58313; 11062, clauses (1)–(3), FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320; 11063, clauses (1)–(3), FR Doc. 2026-18837, 91 FR 58326–58327. September scope changes: 11064, clauses (1)–(2), FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58332; 11065, clauses (1)–(2), FR Doc. 2026-18839, 91 FR 58340. October change: 11076, clauses (1)–(2), FR Doc. 2026-22292, 91 FR 68862. Signature dates appear in each proclamation's heading and execution text; publication dates appear in the cited FR issues.",

  "Q2": {
    "answer": "(a) Section 338 duty:

| Entry | Calculation | Duty |
|---|---|---:|
| 1: August 20, 2:00 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 2: August 21, 11:59 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 3: August 22, 12:01 a.m. | $40,000 × 50% | **$20,000** |

The controlling later provision is clause (1) of 11056, declaring that the effective date “shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026.” The consumption-entry trigger comes from clause (1) of 11046.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 both **declares the new commencement date** and expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of 11046 by replacing August 19 with August 22. It does **not expressly rewrite** the August 19 date printed in numbered clauses (1) and (3), or recital 9, of 11046. The later declaration controls, and clause (5) of 11056 supersedes inconsistent provisions of earlier proclamations to the extent of inconsistency.

(c) The deposited amount was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**, although the section 338 liability was zero. Clause (4) of 11056 provides that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It supplies no special application procedure, deadline, interest rule, or payment timetable.

(d) **No further presidential act was required to start collection on August 22.** Clause (1) of 11056 fixes that date without requiring another finding or proclamation. Later recitals say Canada had expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination; on August 21 it reneged and ceased negotiating in good faith; the three-day suspension then lapsed at 12:01 a.m. on August 22 and the duties became effective. Those are the later proclamations' historical explanations, not additional conditions found in 11056's operative clause.

(e) The original date followed the described statutory minimum of **30 days after the President's proclamation**:

- Signed July 20.
- July 21–31: 11 days.
- August 1–19: 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**, producing August 19.

The original calculation runs from the July 20 proclamation, not its July 23 publication.",

Subsequent history: 11061, recitals 2–4, FR Doc. 2026-18835, 91 FR 58311; also 11064, recitals 2–4, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331.",

    "answer": "(a) The prohibition turns on **importation**, whereas the surviving duty turns on consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal.

| C: imported September 28, 11:30 p.m.; entered September 29, 9:00 a.m. | Permitted: importation preceded September 29, 12:01 a.m.; later entry does not trigger the ban | $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000** |
| D: imported September 29, 12:30 a.m. | **Prohibited** by clause (1); filing an entry that morning does not cure the prohibition | Not a duty-free admission or an admission purchasable by paying 50%; no lawful consumption-entry duty calculation is available on these facts |

(b) **E is a prior import**, because the scenario defines physical arrival on September 25 as importation. The most defensible reading of clause (2) permits its later consumption entry and preserves the 50% duty:

- Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- MFN: $30,000 × 0% = $0.
- Total of those layers: **$15,000**.

The original duty proclamation also requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions, except goods eligible for domestic status, and provides for duty upon consumption entry.

(c) Clause (9)(b) expressly supplies the fallback: if the ban is invalidated as to this import, the **50% duty under 11046 applies** to the imports previously covered by the invalidated prohibition. For a comparable $30,000 shipment: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**. The invalidation does not disturb other bans or additional duties.

(d) **No.** Clause (3) preserves the additional-duty coverage of other products, as otherwise established by the alcoholic-beverages scope proclamation. It does not remove the 50% duty from covered alcoholic products outside the exclusion Annex.",

    "answer": "(a) Applicability of the 50% section 338 duty:

- **P:** Added by September proclamation 11065, Annex I Part A, effective September 15.
- **Q:** Originally covered, but removed by 11065, Part B, effective September 15.
- **R:** Originally covered and not removed in September; removed by October proclamation 11076, **Part A**, effective October 30.
- **S:** Not previously covered; added by 11076, **Part B**, effective October 30. The October Part A/Part B functions are the reverse of September's.

(b) 11076 was **signed October 23**, **filed October 29 at 11:15 a.m.**, and **published October 30**. Its changes apply to consumption entries and warehouse withdrawals for consumption on or after **October 30 at 12:01 a.m.** The scope proclamations do not make these scope changes retroactive and do not provide refunds for otherwise correctly assessed earlier entries. Their effective-date clauses are prospective.

(c) P and S each became dutiable **seven calendar days after the respective scope proclamation was signed**. The recitals describe section 338 as requiring at least 30 days after the President's proclamation finding the discrimination. Q2.answer:
(a) Section 338 duty:

| Entry | Calculation | Duty |
|---|---|---:|
| 1: August 20, 2:00 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 2: August 21, 11:59 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 3: August 22, 12:01 a.m. | $40,000 × 50% | **$20,000** |

The controlling later provision is clause (1) of 11056, declaring that the effective date “shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026.” The consumption-entry trigger comes from clause (1) of 11046.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 both **declares the new commencement date** and expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of 11046 by replacing August 19 with August 22. It does **not expressly rewrite** the August 19 date printed in numbered clauses (1) and (3), or recital 9, of 11046. The later declaration controls, and clause (5) of 11056 supersedes inconsistent provisions of earlier proclamations to the extent of inconsistency.

(c) The deposited amount was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**, although the section 338 liability was zero. Clause (4) of 11056 provides that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It supplies no special application procedure, deadline, interest rule, or payment timetable.

(d) **No further presidential act was required to start collection on August 22.** Clause (1) of 11056 fixes that date without requiring another finding or proclamation. Later recitals say Canada had expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination; on August 21 it reneged and ceased negotiating in good faith; the three-day suspension then lapsed at 12:01 a.m. on August 22 and the duties became effective. Those are the later proclamations' historical explanations, not additional conditions found in 11056's operative clause.

(e) The original date followed the described statutory minimum of **30 days after the President's proclamation**:

- Signed July 20.
- July 21–31: 11 days.
- August 1–19: 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**, producing August 19.

The original calculation runs from the July 20 proclamation, not its July 23 publication.

- Taiwan: $20,000 × 0% = **$0**, because the equivalent rate is at least 10%.
- Switzerland: $20,000 × (12.5% − 11%) = **$300**.

(a) **Printed commencement dates versus the controlling later declaration.** The three originals say their duties and HTSUS changes apply from “August 19, 2026” in clauses (1) and (3): 11046, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46641; 11047, FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46654–46655; 11048, FR Doc. 2026-14997, 91 FR 46665. Thus the originals retain a different printed date; clause (5), 91 FR 54791, resolves the operative inconsistency. This is one common discrepancy, not three separate substantive conflicts.

(b) **The dairy ban cites a dairy scope proclamation that the published series does not contain.** Clause (3) of 11062 describes products “as further established in the Proclamation of September 8, 2026” bearing a dairy scope-modification title: FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320. The actual September scope proclamations are for alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles—11064, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331–58332, and 11065, FR Doc. 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339–58340. The dairy original's operative section 232 exception remains in 11047, clause (2), FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46655. The phantom reference supplies neither a readable new dairy list nor an operative dairy stacking change.

(c) **The presidential memorandum describes the June textile proposal as zero-rated, although the proposal specified only a reduced rate.** The memorandum says USTR proposed a mechanism allowing a volume of textile/apparel imports at “a zero section 301 tariff rate”: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719. The actual June proposal says “a reduced Section 301 tariff rate,” without fixing zero: FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV, 91 FR 34274. This concerns the memorandum's account of the proposal, not merely the later decision to adopt zero-duty TRQs.

(d) **The general ‘net of MFN’ description is incomplete for a Korean special-rate claim.** Memorandum section 1(a)(ii) uses the product's MFN tariff for Korea: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720; the final notice repeats that description at 91 FR 47327, FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.B.49. Operative note 52(k), however, expressly provides an equivalent-rate calculation for a South Korean good on which a specific or compound **column 1-Special** rate is properly claimed, then uses the “applicable column 1 duty rate”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394. This is a qualification not captured by an unqualified MFN-only account; it does not change results where, as in most scenarios here, no special rate is claimed.

(e) **Broad retention language is not a complete account of the adopted categorical exemptions.** The final notice says it determined “not to remove products other than the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed exemption list”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.1, 91 FR 47330. The June readable text proposed a blanket exception for all section 232 articles and parts: FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274 and Annex A introductory notes, 91 FR 34276. The adopted operative note instead states an all-products default, subject to exceptions, and enumerates particular section 232 headings/categories in note 52(f): FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352, 47362–47363. Consequently the broad retention description cannot be used as an operative blanket section 232 exception. This is distinct from—and does not establish an additional image-list deletion beyond—the announced chemical-list narrowing.

(f) **There is also a qualified tension over later exemptions.** The notice says an exclusion process lowering tariffs on additional products “would be inconsistent with the President's direction”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.G, 91 FR 47335. The memorandum's operative section 3(e) expressly says USTR “may modify or terminate the tariffs, exemptions, or TRQs for an economy, as appropriate and subject to my specific direction, if any”: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47722. The notice may be explaining why it declined a process under the current action, but it should not be read as an accurate statement that the memorandum categorically withholds modification authority.

**2 — Incorrect for comments on the proposed action.** Over 450 comments and nearly 60 witnesses concern the earlier investigation/actionability phase and April hearings. [FR Doc. 2026-11296, I, 91 FR 34273; FR Doc. 2026-15181, I and III, 91 FR 47319, 47328; memorandum, FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719.]

**3 — Incorrect.** Six economies are described as subsequently adopting prohibitions—Cambodia, Guatemala, Honduras, India, Sri Lanka and Trinidad and Tobago—and Jordan as undertaking an ART commitment, not adopting a ban. Cambodia and Guatemala already had proposed 10% rates because of ART commitments. The nominal 12.5%-to-10% moves are therefore **Honduras, India, Sri Lanka, Trinidad and Tobago, and Jordan**, not seven ban-adopting economies. [Proposal IV, FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274; final notice I, FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47319; memorandum, FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720.]

**4 — Incorrect.** These were commenter requests, not USTR's adopted disposition. USTR expressly **declined to remove** the products. The beef/forced-labor linkage was attributed to commenters; the avocado discussion concerned domestic competitive pressure. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.3, 91 FR 47331.]

Of those, EU, Taiwan and Switzerland have additional economy-specific product lists; Japan and South Korea do not. Other economies, including the flat-rate UK, also have negotiated exemptions. [Memorandum section 1(a)(ii), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720; final notice III.D, 91 FR 47333, and note 52(j), 91 FR 47363–47394, FR Doc. 2026-15181.]

Note 52(a) affirmatively adds MFN and otherwise applicable additional duties. Even a net-rate economy retains its MFN duty where that duty exceeds the benchmark; the section 301 layer becomes zero rather than reducing MFN. (a) The section 338 presidential series comprises the following ten proclamations. All dates in the table are in 2026; all stated times are Eastern.

| Proclamation; FR document; first-page citation | Signed; published | Operative action and application event |
|---|---|---|
| **11046**; **2026-14991**; **91 FR 46639** | July 20; July 23 | Imposes 50% additional duty on its Annex II Canadian products concerning alcoholic-beverage discrimination. Clauses (1) and (3) originally specify **August 19, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption; 11056 subsequently changes commencement to August 22. |
| **11047**; **2026-14992**; **91 FR 46653** | July 20; July 23 | Corresponding 50% duty concerning dairy discrimination, with the same original **August 19, 12:01 a.m.** consumption-entry/warehouse-withdrawal trigger, subsequently postponed to August 22. |

| **11056**; **2026-17294**; **91 FR 54789** | August 18; August 24 | Postpones all three duties to **August 22, 12:01 a.m.** The underlying consumption-entry/warehouse-withdrawal triggers remain applicable. It expressly replaces the effective date in each original Annex II chapeau. |
| **11061**; **2026-18835**; **91 FR 58311** | September 8; September 14 | Excludes its Annex Canadian alcoholic beverages from importation beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, not consumption entry. Previously imported but unentered goods remain subject to 50% duty. |
| **11062**; **2026-18836**; **91 FR 58319** | September 8; September 14 | Corresponding dairy-related Annex import exclusion beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, with the same prior-import grandfathering. |
| **11063**; **2026-18837**; **91 FR 58325** | September 8; September 14 | Corresponding motor-vehicle-related Annex import exclusion beginning **September 29, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by **importation**, with the same prior-import grandfathering. |
| **11064**; **2026-18838**; **91 FR 58331** | September 8; September 14 | Adds Annex I Part A products to the alcoholic-beverage-related duty, removes Part B products, and makes the duty cumulative with section 232 duties, beginning **September 15, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |
| **11065**; **2026-18839**; **91 FR 58339** | September 8; September 14 | Adds Annex I Part A products to the motor-vehicle-related duty, removes Part B products, and makes the duty cumulative with section 232 duties, beginning **September 15, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |

Applies beginning **October 30, 12:01 a.m.**, measured by consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal for consumption. |

The original three proclamations also have separate foreign-trade-zone provisions governing admission on or after their effective date; those are not the consumption-entry trigger for collecting the duty.

(b) **Product-coverage changes:**

- **Alcoholic-beverage action:** 11046 establishes the original Annex II coverage and readable exceptions; 11064 adds Part A, removes Part B, and eliminates the section 232 non-stacking treatment; 11061 switches its Annex goods from additional-duty treatment to an import prohibition for new imports, while preserving 50% treatment for prior imports.
- **Dairy action:** 11047 establishes original coverage and exceptions; 11062 switches its Annex goods to an import prohibition for new imports. No actual dairy scope-modification proclamation was located. In particular, the original section 232 exception was not removed by a published dairy scope proclamation.
- **Motor-vehicle action:** 11048 establishes original coverage and exceptions; 11065 adds Part A, removes Part B, and permits section 232 stacking; 11063 switches its Annex goods to an import prohibition for new imports; 11076 subsequently removes its Part A and adds its Part B.
- **11056 changes timing, not product coverage.**

Q2.answer:
(a) Section 338 duty:

| Entry | Calculation | Duty |
|---|---|---:|
| 1: August 20, 2:00 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 2: August 21, 11:59 p.m. | $40,000 × 0% during postponement | **$0** |
| 3: August 22, 12:01 a.m. | $40,000 × 50% | **$20,000** |

The controlling later provision is clause (1) of 11056, declaring that the effective date “shall be 12:01 a.m. eastern time on August 22, 2026.” The consumption-entry trigger comes from clause (1) of 11046.

(b) Clause (1) of 11056 both **declares the new commencement date** and expressly amends the **chapeau of Annex II** of 11046 by replacing August 19 with August 22. It does **not expressly rewrite** the August 19 date printed in numbered clauses (1) and (3), or recital 9, of 11046. The later declaration controls, and clause (5) of 11056 supersedes inconsistent provisions of earlier proclamations to the extent of inconsistency.

(c) The deposited amount was $40,000 × 50% = **$20,000**, although the section 338 liability was zero. Clause (4) of 11056 provides that, to the extent implementation requires refunds, they “shall be processed pursuant to applicable law and CBP's standard procedures.” It supplies no special application procedure, deadline, interest rule, or payment timetable.

(d) **No further presidential act was required to start collection on August 22.** Clause (1) of 11056 fixes that date without requiring another finding or proclamation. Later recitals say Canada had expressed a commitment to remove the discrimination; on August 21 it reneged and ceased negotiating in good faith; the three-day suspension then lapsed at 12:01 a.m. on August 22 and the duties became effective. Those are the later proclamations' historical explanations, not additional conditions found in 11056's operative clause.

(e) The original date followed the described statutory minimum of **30 days after the President's proclamation**:

- Signed July 20.
- July 21–31: 11 days.
- August 1–19: 19 days.
- 11 + 19 = **30 days**, producing August 19.

The original calculation runs from the July 20 proclamation, not its July 23 publication.

Q3.answer:
(a) The prohibition turns on **importation**, whereas the surviving duty turns on consumption entry or warehouse withdrawal.

| Shipment | Import treatment | Section 338 duty |
|---|---|---:|
| A: imported September 10; entered September 14 | Permitted; both events precede the ban | $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000** |
| B: imported September 27; warehouse withdrawal October 5 | Permitted under the prior-import rule in clause (2) | $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000** |
| C: imported September 28, 11:30 p.m.; entered September 29, 9:00 a.m. | Permitted: importation preceded September 29, 12:01 a.m.; later entry does not trigger the ban | $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000** |
| D: imported September 29, 12:30 a.m. | **Prohibited** by clause (1); filing an entry that morning does not cure the prohibition | Not a duty-free admission or an admission purchasable by paying 50%; no lawful consumption-entry duty calculation is available on these facts |

(b) **E is a prior import**, because the scenario defines physical arrival on September 25 as importation. The most defensible reading of clause (2) permits its later consumption entry and preserves the 50% duty:

- Section 338: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**.
- MFN: $30,000 × 0% = $0.
- Total of those layers: **$15,000**.

The original duty proclamation also requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions, except goods eligible for domestic status, and provides for duty upon consumption entry.

(c) Clause (9)(b) expressly supplies the fallback: if the ban is invalidated as to this import, the **50% duty under 11046 applies** to the imports previously covered by the invalidated prohibition. For a comparable $30,000 shipment: $30,000 × 50% = **$15,000**. The invalidation does not disturb other bans or additional duties.

(d) **No.** Clause (3) preserves the additional-duty coverage of other products, as otherwise established by the alcoholic-beverages scope proclamation. It does not remove the 50% duty from covered alcoholic products outside the exclusion Annex.

The recitals describe section 338 as requiring at least 30 days after the President's proclamation finding the discrimination. The scope proclamations do not expressly explain how newly added products fit that waiting period. (a) France:

- Ad valorem equivalent: $60 ÷ $12,000 = **0.5%**.

(b) First calculate the compound MFN duty:

- Ad valorem component: $20,000 × 4% = **$800**.
- Specific component: 4,000 kg × $0.25/kg = **$1,000**.
- Column 1-General total: $800 + $1,000 = **$1,800**.
- Equivalent rate: $1,800 ÷ $20,000 = **9%**.

Section 301:

- Italy: $20,000 × (10% − 9%) = **$200**.
- Japan: $20,000 × (12.5% − 9%) = **$700**.
- Brazil: $20,000 × 12.5% = **$2,500**. Brazil has a flat additional rate, not an MFN top-up.

(c) Equivalent MFN rate: $2,200 ÷ $20,000 = **11%**.

- Taiwan: $20,000 × 0% = **$0**, because the equivalent rate is at least 10%.
- Switzerland: $20,000 × (12.5% − 11%) = **$300**.

Q11.answer:
(a) **Printed commencement dates versus the controlling later declaration.** The three originals say their duties and HTSUS changes apply from “August 19, 2026” in clauses (1) and (3): 11046, FR Doc. 2026-14991, 91 FR 46641; 11047, FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46654–46655; 11048, FR Doc. 2026-14997, 91 FR 46665. But 11056, clause (1), declares August 22 and expressly amends only the Annex II chapeaux: FR Doc. 2026-17294, 91 FR 54790. Thus the originals retain a different printed date; clause (5), 91 FR 54791, resolves the operative inconsistency. This is one common discrepancy, not three separate substantive conflicts.

(b) **The dairy ban cites a dairy scope proclamation that the published series does not contain.** Clause (3) of 11062 describes products “as further established in the Proclamation of September 8, 2026” bearing a dairy scope-modification title: FR Doc. 2026-18836, 91 FR 58320. The actual September scope proclamations are for alcoholic beverages and motor vehicles—11064, FR Doc. 2026-18838, 91 FR 58331–58332, and 11065, FR Doc. 2026-18839, 91 FR 58339–58340. The dairy original's operative section 232 exception remains in 11047, clause (2), FR Doc. 2026-14992, 91 FR 46655. The phantom reference supplies neither a readable new dairy list nor an operative dairy stacking change.

(c) **The presidential memorandum describes the June textile proposal as zero-rated, although the proposal specified only a reduced rate.** The memorandum says USTR proposed a mechanism allowing a volume of textile/apparel imports at “a zero section 301 tariff rate”: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47719. The actual June proposal says “a reduced Section 301 tariff rate,” without fixing zero: FR Doc. 2026-11296, section IV, 91 FR 34274. This concerns the memorandum's account of the proposal, not merely the later decision to adopt zero-duty TRQs.

(d) **The general ‘net of MFN’ description is incomplete for a Korean special-rate claim.** Memorandum section 1(a)(ii) uses the product's MFN tariff for Korea: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720; the final notice repeats that description at 91 FR 47327, FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.B.49. Operative note 52(k), however, expressly provides an equivalent-rate calculation for a South Korean good on which a specific or compound **column 1-Special** rate is properly claimed, then uses the “applicable column 1 duty rate”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47394. This is a qualification not captured by an unqualified MFN-only account; it does not change results where, as in most scenarios here, no special rate is claimed.

(e) **Broad retention language is not a complete account of the adopted categorical exemptions.** The final notice says it determined “not to remove products other than the non-pharmaceutical applications of certain products from the proposed exemption list”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.1, 91 FR 47330. The June readable text proposed a blanket exception for all section 232 articles and parts: FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274 and Annex A introductory notes, 91 FR 34276. The adopted operative note instead states an all-products default, subject to exceptions, and enumerates particular section 232 headings/categories in note 52(f): FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47352, 47362–47363. Consequently the broad retention description cannot be used as an operative blanket section 232 exception. This is distinct from—and does not establish an additional image-list deletion beyond—the announced chemical-list narrowing.

(f) **There is also a qualified tension over later exemptions.** The notice says an exclusion process lowering tariffs on additional products “would be inconsistent with the President's direction”: FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.G, 91 FR 47335. The memorandum's operative section 3(e) expressly says USTR “may modify or terminate the tariffs, exemptions, or TRQs for an economy, as appropriate and subject to my specific direction, if any”: FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47722. The notice may be explaining why it declined a process under the current action, but it should not be read as an accurate statement that the memorandum categorically withholds modification authority.

Of those, EU, Taiwan and Switzerland have additional economy-specific product lists; Japan and South Korea do not. Other economies, including the flat-rate UK, also have negotiated exemptions. [Memorandum section 1(a)(ii), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720; final notice III.D, 91 FR 47333, and note 52(j), 91 FR 47363–47394, FR Doc. 2026-15181.]

**6 — Partly correct.** USTR says it excluded **an additional 471 products** in each investigation, but describes **certain** sugar and sugar-containing products, with the explanation discussing **in-quota** imports—not all sugar products. The 471 statement is not a verified net count after narrowing other exemptions. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.D, 91 FR 47331–47333.]

**7 — Incorrect.** The phrase “maximum tariffs of 12.5 percent” in USTR's response concerns this action's tariffs, not an across-the-board total-duty ceiling. Note 52(a) affirmatively adds MFN and otherwise applicable additional duties. Even a net-rate economy retains its MFN duty where that duty exceeds the benchmark; the section 301 layer becomes zero rather than reducing MFN. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.E, 91 FR 47334; note 52(a), 91 FR 47352; memorandum section 1(a)(ii), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47720.]

**8 — Correct for goods subject to this additional duty.** The action determination requires privileged foreign status for covered zone admissions effective when the duty is imposed, except goods eligible for domestic status. It does not impose that requirement on a product exempt from the additional duty. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, II.A, 91 FR 47321.]

**9 — Correct, as the stated severability consequence.** The applicable tariff applies to imports formerly covered by the invalidated exemption; other exemptions and tariff actions remain operative. [Memorandum section 4(e), FR Doc. 2026-15274, 91 FR 47723; final notice IV, FR Doc. 2026-15181, 91 FR 47335.]

**10 — Correct as USTR's express characterization of its Annex A product-list decision, but not independently verifiable from the image tables.** USTR says it retained all proposed Annex A products except non-pharmaceutical applications of certain chemicals. That statement should not be expanded into a claim that every separate categorical exemption in the June proposal survived unchanged: the final section 232 exception is enumerated, not blanket. [FR Doc. 2026-15181, III.C.1–2, 91 FR 47330; note 52(f), 91 FR 47362–47363; June proposal, FR Doc. 2026-11296, 91 FR 34274, 34276.]
